p: The Greek, which places this verse after 15:27, reads 'almsgiving' where the Hebrew has 'loyal love'.

readings.w: Leningrad Codex (AD 1008); Targum; Stuttgart Vulgate ('misericordia et veritate')
Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete), at its 15:27a
readings.en: by almsgiving and acts of faithfulness

why: The Hebrew word is chesed, loyal love, and every Hebrew witness has it. The Greek translator rendered chesed with eleēmosynē, which in his time could mean mercy in general and was coming to mean almsgiving; the difference is one of translation, not of a different Hebrew text. It matters because later Jewish and Christian teaching on almsgiving cited the Greek form (Sirach 3:30; Tobit 12:9).

p: The written text has 'afflicted'; the reading tradition has 'humble'. The words differ by one letter.

readings.w: Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), Qere (the reading tradition); Stuttgart Vulgate ('cum mitibus'); Targum
Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), Ketiv (the consonants as written)

why: Both words come from the same root and are often confused in the Hebrew Bible. 'Humble' matches 'humble in spirit' in the same line and the contrast with 'the proud'; but 'the poor' gives a sharp social point too, being lowly among the poor rather than rich with the proud.

a: a person with a cool spirit
p: The written text says 'cool of spirit'; the reading tradition says 'precious of spirit'. The Plain English Translation follows the written text.

readings.w: Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), Ketiv (the consonants as written)
readings.plain: a person with a cool spirit

readings.w: Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), Qere (the reading tradition); Stuttgart Vulgate ('pretiosi spiritus')
readings.plain: a person with a noble spirit

why: 'Cool' (qar) fits the subject, restraint in speech, and the Egyptian ideal of the 'cool' or silent man against the 'heated' man, a contrast Amenemope draws throughout and Proverbs uses in 15:18 and 22:24. 'Precious of spirit' makes sense but is weaker. The Greek ('long-suffering') and the Targum ('gentle of spirit') paraphrase and do not settle the question.

p: The Greek and the Clementine Latin read 'a good wife' and add a couplet against sending a good wife away; the Hebrew has neither.

readings.w: Leningrad Codex (AD 1008); Targum; Stuttgart Vulgate ('qui invenit mulierem')
Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete); Clementine Vulgate ('mulierem bonam'), as reported
readings.orig: ὃς εὗρεν γυναῖκα ἀγαθήν (hos heuren gynaika agathēn)
readings.en: whoever has found a good wife

why: The Hebrew has no adjective, and its wording matches Wisdom's promise in 8:35, which also has none. The Greek 'good' is an explanation that the saying invites, given the warnings about quarrelsome wives (19:13; 21:9). The Greek also adds (18:22a): 'Whoever casts out a good wife casts out good things, and whoever keeps an adulteress is foolish and ungodly.' The Stuttgart edition of the Vulgate, the critical text of Jerome's Latin, follows the Hebrew here; the Clementine Vulgate, the Latin Bible of the Catholic Church from 1592, is reported to read 'mulierem bonam' and to carry the added couplet, probably from the Old Latin translated from the Greek.

p: The Hebrew says 'a brother offended'. The Greek and the Vulgate read 'a brother helped by a brother', a difference of one letter.

readings.w: Leningrad Codex (AD 1008); Targum ('a brother who rebels against his brother')
Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete); Stuttgart Vulgate ('frater qui adiuvatur a fratre')
readings.orig: ἀδελφὸς ὑπὸ ἀδελφοῦ βοηθούμενος (adelphos hypo adelphou boēthoumenos), implying נוֹשָׁע (nosha')
readings.en: a brother helped by a brother
readings.plain: A brother helped by his brother

why: The Greek and Latin turn the saying into praise of brothers who stand together: 'A brother helped by his brother is like a strong town'. That reading is attractive, but it does not fit the second line, where quarrels are 'like the bolts of a fortress', shutting people out. The Hebrew 'offended' makes the two lines agree: a wronged brother is as hard to win back as a walled town, and the quarrel bars him in. The Targum and Rashi read the Hebrew so.

p: In the third line the written text has lo', 'not'; the reading tradition has lo, 'his'. The Greek has two extra couplets here.

readings.w: Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), Ketiv (the consonants as written); Targum ('not firm'); Stuttgart Vulgate ('nihil habebit')
Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), Qere (the reading tradition)
Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete), its 19:4
readings.orig: ὃς δὲ ἐρεθίζει λόγους οὐ σωθήσεται (hos de erethizei logous ou sōthēsetai)
readings.en: he who provokes with words will not escape

why: The written 'not' gives the best sense: the poor man pleads with his friends and they are no longer there. The reading tradition's 'they are his' is hard to construe. The Greek has three couplets where the Hebrew has a couplet and a single line: the brother-hating couplet, a couplet on good understanding, and one on the evildoer, whose last line seems to render this third line. Many scholars think a line has dropped from the Hebrew.

t: Will die, or will be put to death?
p: The written text has 'will be put to death', the legal formula; the reading tradition has 'will die'.

readings.w: Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), Qere (the reading tradition); Targum ('yemut')
Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), Ketiv (the consonants as written); compare the Stuttgart Vulgate ('mortificabitur')
readings.en: he will be put to death
readings.plain: you will be put to death

why: Wisdom speaks of the outcomes of conduct, not of court sentences, and 'will die' matches the many sayings where the way of folly leads to death (10:21; 15:10). 'Will be put to death' is the formula of the Law (Exodus 21:12–17); the written text may reflect that echo.

p: The reading tradition has 'great of rage'; the written consonants g-r-l are unclear.

readings.w: Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), Qere (the reading tradition)
Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), Ketiv (the consonants as written)

why: The reading tradition gives clear sense; the written form has no certain meaning. The Targum ('a wrathful man') and the Vulgate ('one who is impatient') both give the general sense of the reading tradition.

p: The written text has 'foreigners'; the reading tradition has 'a foreign woman', as does 27:13.

readings.w: Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), Qere (the reading tradition); compare 27:13
Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), Ketiv (the consonants as written); Stuttgart Vulgate ('pro extraneis')

why: The doublet in 27:13 is written with 'a foreign woman' and has no variant, so the reading tradition here makes the two sayings match. 'Foreigners' would be a natural parallel to 'outsider' in the first line, and the Vulgate follows it. The Greek lacks the verse. The 'foreign woman' links the saying to the warnings of chapters 2–7: the man has backed the debt of a woman outside his own household.

p: The written text has ishon, 'pupil, middle'; the reading tradition has eshun, 'time'. Both mean the darkest part of the night.

readings.w: Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), Ketiv (the consonants as written); Stuttgart Vulgate ('in mediis tenebris')
Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), Qere (the reading tradition)

why: The written form is the word of 7:9 ('in the black of night'), and matches the Vulgate's 'in the midst of darkness'. The reading tradition's word is otherwise unknown and may be a by-form of the same word. The sense is the same.

p: The reading tradition has 'hastened'; the written text has a rarer word, perhaps 'gained greedily'.

readings.w: Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), Qere (the reading tradition)
Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), Ketiv (the consonants as written)

why: The reading tradition gives a common word and a clear contrast between 'at the start' and 'at its end', the haste of 13:11 and 28:20. The written word is rare, and its sense is guessed from a single use in Zechariah 11:8. Both describe property got the wrong way; the reading tradition is followed, as in most translations.

t: Seekers of death, or snares of death?
p: The Hebrew has 'seekers of death'. The Greek and Vulgate read 'snares of death', a difference of one letter.

readings.w: Leningrad Codex (AD 1008); Targum
Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete); Stuttgart Vulgate ('ad laqueos mortis')
readings.orig: מוֹקְשֵׁי־מָוֶת (moqshe-mavet), as the Greek and Latin imply

why: 'Snares of death' is a phrase Proverbs uses (13:14; 14:27), which makes it attractive, but it is also the easier reading, and a copyist could have brought it in from those verses. 'Those who seek it are seeking death' is harder but makes sense: the pursuit of wealth by lying is a pursuit of one's own death (compare 8:36).

p: The written text has 'establishes his ways'; the reading tradition 'considers his way'.

readings.w: Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), Qere (the reading tradition); compare the Greek ('understands his ways')
Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), Ketiv (the consonants as written); compare the Stuttgart Vulgate ('corrigit viam suam')

why: The two verbs differ by one letter (b or k). 'Considers' contrasts best with the wicked man's brazen face: one hardens his face, the other thinks. 'Makes his ways firm' also gives good sense, and the Vulgate's 'corrects his way' seems to follow it.

a: Train a young person according to his way
p: The Greek has no 22:6 at all. The Vulgate has it, opening with the words 'It is a proverb'.

readings.w: Leningrad Codex (AD 1008); Targum; Stuttgart Vulgate
readings.orig: חֲנֹךְ לַנַּעַר עַל־פִּי דַרְכּוֹ (chanokh lanna'ar 'al-pi darko)
readings.en: train a youth according to his way
readings.plain: Train a young person according to his way

readings.w: Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete)

why: The verse is in every Hebrew witness, the Targum and the Vulgate. Its absence from the Greek is one of several gaps in Greek Proverbs in these chapters (18:23–19:2; 20:14–19; 21:5), and probably reflects the translator's or his source's choices, not a shorter original Hebrew. The Vulgate's opening words, 'proverbium est', 'it is a proverb', have no counterpart in the Hebrew.

a: the rod he swung in his rage will come to an end
t: A Greek addition: the cheerful giver
p: After this verse the Greek adds a couplet, 'God blesses a cheerful man and a giver', which Paul seems to echo.

readings.w: Leningrad Codex (AD 1008); Targum; Stuttgart Vulgate
readings.en: the rod of his fury will fail
readings.plain: the rod he swung in his rage will come to an end

readings.w: Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete), 22:8a, added after the verse
readings.orig: ἄνδρα ἱλαρὸν καὶ δότην εὐλογεῖ ὁ θεός, ματαιότητα δὲ ἔργων αὐτοῦ συντελέσει (andra hilaron kai dotēn eulogei ho theos, mataiotēta de ergōn autou syntelesei)
readings.en: God blesses a cheerful man and a giver, and he will bring to an end the futility of his works
readings.plain: the rod he swung in his rage will come to an end / God blesses a cheerful man and a giver, and will finish the emptiness of his works

why: The added couplet is not in any Hebrew witness, the Targum or the Stuttgart Vulgate. It may be a second rendering of the Hebrew verse that came into the Greek alongside the first: its second line nearly repeats the Greek of 22:8b. Paul's 'God loves a cheerful giver' (2 Corinthians 9:7) is close to its first line, and he may have had it in mind.

p: The written text has 'formerly', the reading tradition 'officers' or 'excellent things'. Most modern scholars read 'thirty', matching Amenemope.

readings.w: Conjectural emendation (no manuscript): the written consonants read as שְׁלֹשִׁים (sheloshim), 'thirty'; proposed after the Amenemope parallel was found (1924) and followed by most modern translations
Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), Qere (the reading tradition); KJV ('excellent things')
Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), Ketiv (the consonants as written)
Greek (Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete); Stuttgart Vulgate ('tripliciter'); Targum ('three times')
readings.en: three times, in a threefold way

why: Amenemope's last chapter begins 'Behold the Thirty Chapters!', and Proverbs 22:17–23:11 has its closest parallels to him. With the same consonants as the written text (sh-l-sh-m) the word can be read 'thirty', and the following section can be divided into about thirty units, though scholars count them differently. 'Formerly' (shilshom) is elsewhere always paired with 'yesterday'; 'officers' makes little sense here. The ancient versions saw a form of 'three' but did not know the Egyptian work. The reading 'thirty' is a scholarly proposal, not attested in any manuscript.
